cards.front: What are simultaneous equations?
cards.back: Two or more equations that must be true at the same time.

options.text: Two or more equations that must be true at the same time.
options.explanation: Simultaneous equations form a set whose equations must all hold for the same values of the variables, so they must be true at the same time.

options.text: Two or more equations that must be solved separately from each other.
options.explanation: Solving each equation with unrelated values misses the defining requirement. Simultaneous equations are two or more equations that must be true at the same time.

options.text: Two or more equations that must have exactly the same coefficients.
options.explanation: Equations do not need identical coefficients to be simultaneous. They are simultaneous when the same variable values must make all the equations true at the same time.

options.text: Two or more equations that must use completely different variables.
options.explanation: Having different variables does not define simultaneous equations. The equations usually share variables and must all be satisfied by the same values at the same time.

cards.front: What does the solution to a pair of simultaneous equations represent on a graph?
cards.back: The coordinates of the point where the two lines intersect.

options.text: The coordinates of the point where the two lines intersect.
options.explanation: A solution satisfies both equations, so its coordinates lie on both lines. Graphically, this is precisely the point at which the two lines intersect.

options.text: The gradients of the two lines where they have the same steepness.
options.explanation: The gradient describes a line’s steepness, not the shared solution. The solution is given by the coordinates of the point where the two lines intersect.

options.text: The intercepts of the points where the two lines cross the axes.
options.explanation: The intercepts show where individual lines cross an axis, which is not generally their shared solution. The solution is the coordinates of the lines’ intersection point.

options.text: The coordinates of the point lying exactly between both lines.
options.explanation: The midpoint between two lines need not lie on either line and does not satisfy both equations. The solution is the coordinates of their intersection point.

cards.front: How do you verify if a pair of values (e.g., $x=4, y=1$) is the correct solution?
cards.back: Substitute the values into both original equations to see if they work.

options.text: Substitute the values into both original equations to see if they work.
options.explanation: A simultaneous solution must satisfy every original equation. Substituting both values into both equations confirms whether each resulting numerical statement is true.

options.text: Substitute the values into one original equation to see if they work.
options.explanation: Checking only one equation can accept values that fail the other equation. Substitute the values into both original equations and verify that both statements are true.

options.text: Add the values together in both original equations to see if they work.
options.explanation: Adding the values together does not test whether they satisfy either equation. Each value must be substituted for its variable in both original equations.

options.text: Swap the values before using both original equations to see if they work.
options.explanation: Swapping the values tests the ordered pair $(y,x)$ rather than the proposed pair $(x,y)$. Substitute each value for its correct variable in both equations.

cards.front: Elimination means adding or subtracting equations so that [ ___ ].
cards.back: Elimination means adding or subtracting equations so that one variable disappears.

options.text: one variable disappears
options.explanation: Adding or subtracting suitably arranged equations cancels matching variable terms. This makes one variable disappear, leaving an equation in the remaining variable.

options.text: both variables remain
options.explanation: Elimination aims to remove a variable, not preserve both of them. The equations are added or subtracted so that one variable disappears.

options.text: each variable is isolated
options.explanation: Adding or subtracting equations does not generally isolate each variable immediately. Elimination first makes one variable disappear so the remaining variable can be found.

options.text: one coefficient doubles
options.explanation: A coefficient can double when like-signed terms are added, but that is not the aim of elimination. The operation should make one variable disappear.

cards.front: What is a coefficient in algebra?
cards.back: The number multiplying a variable (e.g., in $4x$, the coefficient is $4$).

options.text: The number multiplying a variable (e.g., in $4x$, the coefficient is $4$).
options.explanation: A coefficient is the numerical factor attached to a variable. For example, $4x$ means $4\times x$, so its coefficient is $4$.

options.text: The letter representing a number (e.g., in $4x$, the coefficient is $x$).
options.explanation: The variable is the letter representing an unknown quantity, not the coefficient. In $4x$, the number $4$ multiplies $x$ and is therefore the coefficient.

options.text: The power applied to a variable (e.g., in $4x$, the coefficient is $1$).
options.explanation: An exponent indicates repeated multiplication and is written as a power, whereas a coefficient multiplies a variable. In $4x$, the coefficient is $4$.

options.text: The constant without a variable (e.g., in $4x$, the coefficient is $x$).
options.explanation: A constant term has no variable attached, whereas a coefficient is the number multiplying a variable. In $4x$, that multiplying number is $4$.

cards.front: In the elimination method, when should you add the two equations?
cards.back: When the coefficients of a variable are the same size but have opposite signs (e.g., $+2y$ and $-2y$).

options.text: When the coefficients of a variable are the same size but have opposite signs (e.g., $+2y$ and $-2y$).
options.explanation: Equal-sized coefficients with opposite signs cancel when added, since terms such as $+2y$ and $-2y$ sum to zero. This eliminates that variable.

options.text: When the coefficients of a variable are the same size and have the same sign (e.g., $+2y$ and $+2y$).
options.explanation: Equal-sized coefficients with the same sign double when added rather than cancelling. In this case, subtract the equations to eliminate the variable.

options.text: When the coefficients of a variable are different sizes but have opposite signs (e.g., $+2y$ and $-3y$).
options.explanation: Opposite signs alone do not guarantee cancellation when the coefficient sizes differ. First scale an equation so the coefficients have the same size, then add.

options.text: When the coefficients of a variable are different sizes and have the same sign (e.g., $+2y$ and $+3y$).
options.explanation: Different-sized coefficients with the same sign do not cancel through addition. The equations must first be scaled to create equal-sized coefficients suitable for elimination.

cards.front: In the elimination method, when should you subtract the two equations?
cards.back: When the coefficients of a variable are the same size and have the same sign (e.g., $+3y$ and $+3y$).

options.text: When the coefficients of a variable are the same size and have the same sign (e.g., $+3y$ and $+3y$).
options.explanation: Equal-sized coefficients with the same sign cancel when one equation is subtracted from the other, since terms such as $+3y-(+3y)$ equal zero.

options.text: When the coefficients of a variable are the same size but have opposite signs (e.g., $+3y$ and $-3y$).
options.explanation: Subtracting equal-sized terms with opposite signs makes their size double rather than cancelling them. Add the equations when the coefficients have opposite signs.

options.text: When the coefficients of a variable are different sizes and have the same sign (e.g., $+3y$ and $+2y$).
options.explanation: Same signs alone are insufficient when the coefficient sizes differ, because subtraction leaves a non-zero variable term. First scale an equation to make the sizes equal.

options.text: When the coefficients of a variable are different sizes and have opposite signs (e.g., $+3y$ and $-2y$).
options.explanation: Different-sized coefficients with opposite signs do not cancel through subtraction. Scale the equations to equalise their sizes, then add terms with opposite signs.

cards.front: If the coefficients of a variable have the [ ___ ], you subtract the equations; if they have opposite signs, you add them.
cards.back: If the coefficients of a variable have the same sign, you subtract the equations; if they have opposite signs, you add them.

options.text: same sign
options.explanation: Coefficients with the same sign cancel through subtraction because one is removed from the other. Coefficients with opposite signs instead cancel through addition.

options.text: same size
options.explanation: Coefficient size alone does not determine the operation because signs also matter. Subtract equal coefficients with the same sign, but add equal-sized coefficients with opposite signs.

options.text: opposite sign
options.explanation: Coefficients with opposite signs should be added, not subtracted, so that they cancel. Subtraction is used when equal-sized coefficients have the same sign.

options.text: same variable
options.explanation: Both equations normally contain the same variable regardless of which operation is needed. Subtract when its equal-sized coefficients have the same sign, and add when they have opposite signs.

cards.front: If the coefficients of a variable have the same sign, you subtract the equations; if they have [ ___ ], you add them.
cards.back: If the coefficients of a variable have the same sign, you subtract the equations; if they have opposite signs, you add them.

options.text: opposite signs
options.explanation: Opposite signs cancel when the equations are added because one coefficient is positive and the other is negative.

options.text: the same signs
options.explanation: Coefficients with the same signs reinforce rather than cancel when added. The correct fill is opposite signs, because a positive and negative coefficient cancel through addition.

options.text: positive signs
options.explanation: Two positive coefficients become larger when added, so the variable is not eliminated. The correct fill is opposite signs, which cancel when the equations are added.

options.text: negative signs
options.explanation: Two negative coefficients combine rather than cancel when added. The correct fill is opposite signs, because equal positive and negative coefficients sum to zero.

cards.front: What is the common mistake when subtracting one equation from another?
cards.back: Forgetting to subtract every term on both the left and right sides of the equals sign.

options.text: Forgetting to subtract every term on both the left and right sides of the equals sign.
options.explanation: Subtracting equations means subtracting the entire second equation, so every term on both sides must have the subtraction applied to it.

options.text: Forgetting to divide every term on both the left and right sides of the equals sign.
options.explanation: Division is not the required operation when one equation is being subtracted. The common mistake is failing to subtract every term on both sides of the equals sign.

options.text: Forgetting to multiply every term on both the left and right sides of the equals sign.
options.explanation: Multiplication is used earlier only when coefficients need matching. During subtraction, the key mistake is forgetting to subtract every term on both sides of the equations.

options.text: Forgetting to substitute every term on both the left and right sides of the equals sign.
options.explanation: Substitution is a different solving method and is not applied term by term here. When subtracting equations, every term on both sides must be subtracted.

cards.front: What must be done if neither $x$ nor $y$ have matching coefficients in a pair of equations?
cards.back: Multiply one or both whole equations by a number to make the coefficients match.

options.text: Multiply one or both whole equations by a number to make the coefficients match.
options.explanation: Multiplying a whole equation preserves its equality while producing matching coefficients, allowing one variable to be eliminated by adding or subtracting the equations.

options.text: Add a number to one or both equations to make the coefficients match.
options.explanation: Adding a number does not scale the coefficients and may alter only selected terms. Instead, multiply one or both whole equations to create matching coefficients.

options.text: Multiply only the variable terms by a number to make the coefficients match.
options.explanation: Multiplying only variable terms changes the equation and destroys the equality. Every term in one or both whole equations must be multiplied by the chosen number.

options.text: Swap the variables in one or both equations to make the coefficients match.
options.explanation: Swapping variables changes what the equations represent and does not produce an equivalent system. Multiply one or both whole equations to make corresponding coefficients match.

cards.front: When multiplying an equation to match coefficients, [ ___ ] in the equation must be multiplied by that number.
cards.back: When multiplying an equation to match coefficients, every term in the equation must be multiplied by that number.

options.text: every term
options.explanation: An equation remains balanced only if the multiplier is applied to every term on both sides, including variables, constants and any negative terms.

options.text: only the variable term
options.explanation: Multiplying only the variable term changes the equation rather than forming an equivalent one. The correct fill is every term, including constants on both sides.

options.text: only the coefficient
options.explanation: Changing only one coefficient does not preserve the equality of the original equation. The correct fill is every term, all multiplied by the same number.

options.text: the term being eliminated
options.explanation: Scaling only the term intended for elimination produces a non-equivalent equation. The correct fill is every term, because the whole equation must be multiplied consistently.

cards.front: What is the standard form for arranging simultaneous equations before solving?
cards.back: $$ax + by = c$ (variables on the left, number on the right).

options.text: $$ax + by = c$ (variables on the left, number on the right).
options.explanation: Standard form places both variable terms together on the left-hand side and the constant alone on the right-hand side.

options.text: $$c = ax + by$ (number on the left, variables on the right).
options.explanation: Although algebraically equivalent, this reverses the required standard arrangement. Standard form is $ax + by = c$, with variables left and the constant right.

options.text: $$ax = c - by$ ($x$ on the left, $y$ and number on the right).
options.explanation: This leaves the variable terms on opposite sides of the equation. Standard form collects both variables on the left as $ax + by = c$.

options.text: $$by = c - ax$ ($y$ on the left, $x$ and number on the right).
options.explanation: This isolates one variable term instead of collecting both on the same side. Standard form is $ax + by = c$, with the constant on the right.

cards.front: How should the equation $3x = 12 + y$ be rearranged into standard form?

options.explanation: Subtracting $y$ from both sides moves it to the left with a negative sign, leaving the constant $12$ on the right.
This keeps $y$ positive after moving it across the equals sign. Subtracting $y$ from both sides gives the correct form $3x - y = 12$.
The sign of $12$ should not change because it has not crossed the equals sign. Only $y$ moves, giving $3x - y = 12$.
This incorrectly changes the signs of both $y$ and $12$. Subtract only $y$ from both sides to obtain $3x - y = 12$.

cards.front: If solving simultaneous equations results in a fractional answer, you should [ ___ ] as not all answers are whole numbers.
cards.back: If solving simultaneous equations results in a fractional answer, you should keep going carefully as not all answers are whole numbers.

options.text: keep going carefully
options.explanation: Simultaneous equations can legitimately have fractional solutions, so continue using exact fraction arithmetic and check the final values in both original equations.

options.text: round it immediately
options.explanation: Rounding during the calculation loses accuracy and may prevent the solution satisfying both equations. The correct fill is keep going carefully, retaining the exact fraction.

options.text: change it to zero
options.explanation: A fractional value is not automatically zero and replacing it changes the solution. The correct fill is keep going carefully, because fractional answers can be valid.

options.text: start again completely
options.explanation: A fraction does not by itself show that an error has occurred. The correct fill is keep going carefully, while checking each algebraic step and sign.

cards.front: After finding the value of one variable (e.g., $x=4$), how do you find the value of the second variable?
cards.back: Substitute the known value into one of the original equations and solve.

options.text: Substitute the known value into one of the original equations and solve.
options.explanation: Replacing the known variable in either original equation leaves an equation containing only the second variable, which can then be solved directly.

options.text: Substitute the known value into the final one-variable equation and solve.
options.explanation: The final one-variable equation only confirms the value already found and contains no second variable. Substitute into one original equation to calculate the other value.

options.text: Add the known value to both of the original equations and solve.
options.explanation: Adding the value changes the equations and does not replace the known variable. Substitute it into one original equation, leaving only the second variable unknown.

options.text: Divide both original equations by the known value and solve.
options.explanation: Dividing the equations does not use the fact that one variable has a known value. Substitute that value into one original equation and solve for the other variable.

cards.front: Two sandwiches ($s$) and three drinks ($d$) cost £14.70. One sandwich and two drinks cost £8.70. What are the two equations?

options.explanation: The coefficients represent the numbers of sandwiches and drinks in each purchase, while £14.70 and £8.70 are the corresponding totals.
This swaps the two purchase totals. The order information gives $2s + 3d = 14.70$ for the first purchase and $s + 2d = 8.70$ for the second.
This reverses the numbers of sandwiches and drinks in both purchases. The correct coefficients are two and three in the first equation, then one and two in the second.
The second purchase has one sandwich and two drinks, not two sandwiches and one drink. Its equation must therefore be $s + 2d = 8.70$.

cards.front: In word problems, it is vital not to [ ___ ] of your variables halfway through the calculation.
cards.back: In word problems, it is vital not to swap the meanings of your variables halfway through the calculation.

options.text: swap the meanings
options.explanation: Each variable must represent the same quantity throughout the calculation. Swapping their meanings would make later equations and substitutions inconsistent with the original definitions.

options.text: swap the coefficients
options.explanation: Coefficients may legitimately change when equations are multiplied during elimination. The essential rule is not to swap the meanings assigned to the variables themselves.

options.text: reverse the signs
options.explanation: Signs can legitimately reverse when multiplying an entire equation by a negative number. The key consistency requirement is not to swap the meanings of the variables.

options.text: simplify the coefficients
options.explanation: Simplifying coefficients can be a valid algebraic step when applied correctly. The mistake warned against is swapping the meanings of the variables during the calculation.

cards.front: How do you perform a final check of your answers for $x$ and $y$?
cards.back: Substitute both values into both original equations to ensure both sides match.

options.text: Substitute both values into both original equations to ensure both sides match.
options.explanation: A simultaneous solution must satisfy both original equations. Substituting both values into each equation confirms that every left-hand side equals its corresponding right-hand side.

options.text: Substitute both values into one original equation to ensure both sides match.
options.explanation: Checking only one equation can miss a pair that satisfies that equation but not the other. Both values must be substituted into both original equations.

options.text: Substitute one value into both original equations to ensure both sides match.
options.explanation: Each original equation contains both unknowns, so checking only one value is incomplete. Substitute both values into both equations and verify that the two sides match.

options.text: Substitute both values into the final equation only to ensure both sides match.
options.explanation: A final derived equation may not independently check the original system. Both calculated values must be substituted into both original equations to verify the solution fully.

cards.front: A pair of values is only a solution if it works in [ ___ ] equations.
cards.back: A pair of values is only a solution if it works in both equations.

options.text: both
options.explanation: Simultaneous equations require one pair of values that satisfies the two equations at the same time. Therefore, the pair must work in both equations.

options.text: only one of the
options.explanation: Satisfying just one equation does not establish a simultaneous solution because many other pairs may also satisfy it. The values must work in both equations.

options.text: at least one of the
options.explanation: Working in at least one equation is insufficient for a simultaneous solution. The defining requirement is that the same pair of values satisfies both equations.

options.text: neither of the
options.explanation: A pair that satisfies neither equation cannot be a solution to the system. A valid simultaneous solution must make both original equations true.

cards.front: In the standard form $ax+by=c$, the [ ___ ] is placed on the right side of the equation.
cards.back: In the standard form $ax+by=c$, the constant (number) is placed on the right side of the equation.

options.text: constant (number)
options.explanation: In $ax+by=c$, the variable terms are collected on the left and the constant value $c$, which contains no variable, is placed on the right.

options.text: coefficient of x
options.explanation: The coefficient of $x$ is $a$, and it remains attached to $x$ on the left. The constant $c$ is placed alone on the right.

options.text: coefficient of y
options.explanation: The coefficient of $y$ is $b$, which forms the term $by$ on the left. It is the constant $c$ that belongs on the right.

options.text: variable term
options.explanation: The variable terms $ax$ and $by$ are placed on the left in standard form. The constant number $c$ is isolated on the right.
